intro: Welcome to C2 reading! At C1 you labelled arguments and spotted bias in reports and opinion pieces. Now you read the hardest texts of all: literature, philosophical essays and ironic columns, where the meaning sits in what is implied, in the narrator's voice and in the writer's style.
teachingNotes: Build on c1-reading-complex (claim, reasons, evidence, counter-argument and rebuttal; loaded words and bias; does the evidence support the claim?) and b2-reading-strategies (inference = what is implied, tone words, irony only recognised): recap in one line, don't re-teach. New at C2: literary texts, philosophical essays and satirical columns, and explaining HOW the style creates the tone. COPYRIGHT: every extract in this lesson is an original practice text written for it and labelled as such. You may name famous works as examples of a style (Swift's A Modest Proposal, Orwell's Animal Farm, Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day, Pramoedya's Bumi Manusia), but never quote real literature, columns or essays beyond a few words: write a new extract in the same style instead. Every answer comes from the words in the text, never from the learner's own opinion.

Literary texts: the narrator (who tells the story) is not the author. First-person narrator (I, we: Indonesian 'sudut pandang orang pertama, aku-an'), third-person narrator (he, she, they: 'dia-an'); an omniscient narrator knows every character's thoughts; an unreliable narrator's words clash with their own actions or with facts (I'm the most patient manager in the building… I only mentioned it three times). Characters are shown through action and dialogue rather than told ('It's fine,' he said, without looking up = it isn't fine). Imagery = words for what we see, hear, smell, touch; a symbol = a concrete thing that stands for an idea (a shutter coming down = an ending). Implied meaning: ask what a detail suggests and which words show it. Indonesian bridge: learners met 'majas' at school (metafora, simile/perumpamaan, personifikasi, hiperbola, ironi, repetisi) and 'suasana' in cerpen. Common errors: treating the narrator's opinion as the author's or as the truth; over-reading every object as a symbol (a symbol needs support: it is repeated, placed at a key moment or linked to the theme); stating an implied meaning with no words to support it.

Philosophical essays: abstract arguments built from moves, each with signposts: definition (By X I mean…, Let us call…), thought experiment (Imagine…, Suppose…, Consider a case in which…), objection (It might be objected that…, Some will say…, A critic may reply…), reply (I grant that… but…, This objection fails because…, But this assumes…), conclusion (It follows that…, If this is right, then…). Read slowly and paraphrase each paragraph in one plain sentence; watch the former / the latter and conclusions in an 'if… then' form, which claim less than they seem to. Common errors: taking an objection (It might be objected that…) as the writer's own view (the C1 counter-argument trap again); reading 'I grant that' as agreement with the whole objection (it concedes a small point before the reply); losing the thread in long abstract nouns instead of asking 'what does this sentence DO in the argument?'.

Satire and irony in columns: satire mocks a real problem to make a serious point. Techniques: saying the opposite of what you mean (irony), exaggeration to absurdity, a mock-serious (deadpan) tone: absurd proposals in calm, official language (I therefore propose a modest solution…, apply online for a Crossing Permit). Clues: an absurd headline, proposals no one could mean, contradictions, absurd logic, a real problem described as a good thing, and the writer's name on a known humour column. 'A modest proposal' is a nod to Jonathan Swift's 1729 essay A Modest Proposal (name it, explain it, don't quote it). The real point is usually the opposite of the literal proposal (ban pedestrians → protect pedestrians). The danger: reading satire literally, sharing a satirical piece as real news, or getting angry at the writer. Indonesian bridge: sindiran, majas ironi / sinisme / sarkasme. British pavement = American sidewalk (both fine). Common errors: deciding from one positive word that a text is ironic (check the whole text against the facts); naming the literal proposal as the writer's view; missing that satire attacks the problem, not the victims.

Author's style: sentence length and rhythm (short sentences = tension, shock, finality; long, flowing sentences = memory, calm, overwhelm), word choice and register (warm, everyday, technical, official, slang), figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification), repetition, and point of view. They create the tone (the writer's attitude: nostalgic, bitter, playful, detached, critical) and the mood (how the reader feels: tense, peaceful). A good answer names the feature AND its effect, and quotes the words. Common errors: naming a tone with no evidence; confusing tone (the writer's attitude) with mood (the reader's feeling); calling any calm text 'detached' or any sad text 'bitter' (bitter = angry and blaming someone).

Limits: no new grammar (every structure is available at C2; the point is control and interpretation). Don't teach literary theory beyond this lesson's terms (no metre, no schools of criticism, no Horatian/Juvenalian labels), and don't give opinions on real politicians: satire practice targets civic problems (traffic, fees, floods, meetings). Interpretation is partly judgement, so test only clear cases: one answer clearly supported by the words, distractors clearly unsupported. Typed answers: accept any wording with the same meaning; an answer in Indonesian shows understanding, but ask for the English word.

keyPoints.title: Reading literature and philosophical essays
keyPoints.explanation: In literature, ask who is telling the story (first person or third person) and whether you can trust them: an unreliable narrator's words clash with their own actions. Writers show character through actions and dialogue, use imagery and symbols, and leave much implied: ask what a detail suggests and which words show it. In a philosophical essay, follow the moves (definition, thought experiment, objection, reply, conclusion) through their signposts, read slowly and paraphrase each paragraph in one plain sentence.

examples.en: 'It's fine,' said Pak Hasan, without looking up from his phone.
examples.id: 'Nggak apa-apa,' kata Pak Hasan, tanpa mengangkat wajah dari HP-nya. (ditunjukkan lewat tindakan: sebenarnya ada apa-apa)

examples.en: Suppose you could read every thought of the people around you.
examples.id: Misalkan kamu bisa membaca setiap pikiran orang di sekitarmu. (thought experiment)

examples.en: It might be objected that this is unfair.
examples.id: Mungkin ada yang menyanggah bahwa ini tidak adil. (objection: pandangan pihak lain, bukan penulis)

id.title: Membaca karya sastra dan esai filosofis
id.explanation: Dalam karya sastra, tanyakan siapa yang bercerita (orang pertama atau orang ketiga) dan apakah dia bisa dipercaya: kata-kata narator yang tidak bisa dipercaya (unreliable narrator) bertentangan dengan tindakannya sendiri. Penulis menunjukkan tokoh lewat tindakan dan dialog, memakai citraan (imagery) dan simbol, dan banyak hal dibiarkan tersirat: tanyakan apa yang disiratkan sebuah detail dan kata mana yang menunjukkannya. Dalam esai filosofis, ikuti langkah-langkahnya (definisi, eksperimen pikiran, sanggahan, jawaban, kesimpulan) lewat kata penandanya, baca pelan-pelan dan parafrasekan setiap paragraf dalam satu kalimat sederhana.

keyPoints.title: Reading ironic and satirical columns
keyPoints.explanation: Satire mocks a real problem to make a serious point. It says the opposite of what it means, exaggerates until the idea is absurd and keeps a mock-serious tone: a crazy proposal in calm, official language. Clues: an absurd headline, proposals nobody could mean, contradictions and absurd logic. The real point is usually the opposite of the literal proposal. The danger is reading satire literally: sharing it as news or getting angry at the writer.

examples.en: I therefore propose a modest solution: close all the parks, so that nobody can complain about them.
examples.id: Karena itu saya mengusulkan solusi sederhana: tutup semua taman, supaya tidak ada yang bisa mengeluhkannya. (usul absurd dengan bahasa resmi)

examples.en: What a triumph: the new bus lane is finished, and the buses still can't use it.
examples.id: Sungguh sebuah kemenangan: jalur bus yang baru sudah selesai, dan bus-busnya tetap tidak bisa memakainya. (ironi: maksudnya proyek itu gagal)

id.title: Membaca kolom yang ironis dan satir
id.explanation: Satire mengejek masalah nyata untuk menyampaikan maksud yang serius. Satire mengatakan kebalikan dari maksudnya, melebih-lebihkan sampai idenya absurd, dan memakai nada pura-pura serius: usul yang gila dengan bahasa yang tenang dan resmi. Petunjuknya: judul yang absurd, usul yang tidak mungkin dimaksudkan sungguh-sungguh, kontradiksi dan logika yang absurd. Maksud sebenarnya biasanya kebalikan dari usul harfiahnya. Bahayanya adalah membaca satire secara harfiah: membagikannya sebagai berita atau marah kepada penulisnya.

keyPoints.title: How style creates meaning and tone
keyPoints.explanation: Style is how a writer writes: sentence length and rhythm, word choice and register, figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification), repetition and point of view. These choices create the tone, the writer's attitude (nostalgic, bitter, playful, detached, critical), and the mood, how the reader feels. Short sentences build tension; long, flowing ones suit memory. A good answer names the feature, its effect, and the words that show it.

examples.en: The lights went out. Then the phones. Then the voices.
examples.id: Lampu padam. Lalu ponsel. Lalu suara-suara. (kalimat sangat pendek = tegang)

examples.en: The old market smelled of cloves, wet earth and my mother's hands.
examples.id: Pasar lama itu beraroma cengkih, tanah basah dan tangan ibuku. (citraan bau + kenangan = nostalgia)

id.title: Bagaimana gaya membangun makna dan nada
id.explanation: Gaya adalah cara penulis menulis: panjang dan irama kalimat, pilihan kata dan ragam bahasa (register), bahasa kiasan (simile, metafora, personifikasi), pengulangan, dan sudut pandang. Pilihan-pilihan ini membangun nada (tone), yaitu sikap penulis (nostalgic, bitter, playful, detached, critical), dan suasana (mood), yaitu apa yang dirasakan pembaca. Kalimat pendek membangun ketegangan; kalimat panjang yang mengalir cocok untuk kenangan. Jawaban yang baik menyebut cirinya, efeknya, dan kata-kata yang menunjukkannya.

guidedPractice.prompt: Who tells this story: a first-person or a third-person narrator? 'Sari pretended to read the menu while her father counted the money in his wallet for the second time.'
guidedPractice.hint: Look at the pronouns: is there an 'I', or only 'she', 'her' and 'his'?

guidedPractice.prompt: In an essay, a philosopher writes: 'Suppose you could take a pill that made you feel happy for the rest of your life, although nothing in your life really changed. Would you take it?' Which move is this: definition, thought experiment or objection?
guidedPractice.hint: 'Suppose…' asks you to imagine an invented case and test your intuition on it.

guidedPractice.prompt: A column begins: 'Good news for Semarang: after this year's floods, the city has finally found a strategy that costs nothing. It is called hoping.' What does the writer really think of the city's flood plans? Choose one: excellent, cheap, non-existent.
guidedPractice.hint: Is 'hoping' really a strategy? The writer praises it, but means the opposite.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which tone word fits best: critical, nostalgic or playful? 'The minister thanked everyone for their patience. The bridge, he said, would open soon. He had said the same thing in 2019, in 2021 and again in 2023.'
guidedPractice.hint: The last sentence adds a fact without comment. What does it make you think of the minister's promise?

independentPractice.prompt: In an essay you read: 'I grant that money matters; but a life spent only earning it is not a free life.' Does the writer accept the whole objection, or concede a small point before replying?
expected: concede a small point before replying
concedes a small point before replying
the writer concedes a small point
independentPractice.hint: 'I grant that…, but…' = 'Memang…, tetapi…'. What comes after 'but'?

independentPractice.prompt: A satirical company newsletter says: 'Management has solved burnout. From Monday, the word tired is banned in all meetings. The 11 p.m. meetings will continue as normal.' What does the writer really think causes the burnout?
independentPractice.hint: Banning a word changes nothing. Which detail in the last sentence is the real problem?

independentPractice.prompt: Which feature of style creates the rhythm in this sentence? 'She waited through the rains, through two elections, through the birth of a grandson she never met.'
independentPractice.hint: Which word comes back again and again?

assessment.prompt: Read this practice text (an original extract written for this lesson). 'Nobody could call me careless with money. This year I bought only three phones, each of them a bargain, and I cancelled my gym membership the moment I noticed I had not been for eleven months. My sister keeps telling me to make a budget. I don't need one: I remember everything I spend, roughly.' What kind of narrator is this? Choose one: omniscient narrator, reliable narrator, unreliable narrator.
assessment.rubric: Correct: unreliable narrator: the narrator's words ('Nobody could call me careless with money', 'I remember everything I spend') clash with their own actions (three phones in a year, eleven months of gym fees for nothing) and with the last word 'roughly'. 'first-person narrator' alone = 40 (true, but it misses the clash between words and actions that the question is about). 'reliable narrator' = 0. 'omniscient narrator' = 0 (an omniscient narrator knows every character's thoughts; this is one person talking about themselves). The idea in Indonesian ('narator yang tidak bisa dipercaya') = 50: ask for the English term.

assessment.prompt: Read this extract from a philosophical essay (an original practice text). '(A) By a promise I mean words that give another person the right to expect something from us. (B) Suppose you promise a dying friend that you will scatter his ashes at sea, and afterwards you simply keep them on a shelf. (C) Some will say that nothing wrong has happened, since your friend can no longer be disappointed. (D) But this assumes that promises matter only because of how people feel; if that were true, a secret betrayal would be no betrayal at all.' Which move in the argument is sentence (C)? Choose one: definition, thought experiment, objection, reply.
assessment.rubric: Correct: objection: 'Some will say that…' introduces a view against the writer's position (nobody is harmed, so nothing is wrong); it is not the writer's own view. 'counter-argument' (the C1 term) = 100. 'reply' = 0: the reply is (D), which starts with 'But this assumes…'. 'thought experiment' = 0: that is (B), 'Suppose…'. 'definition' = 0: that is (A), 'By a promise I mean…'.

assessment.prompt: Read this practice text (an original short extract). 'When the letter from the hospital came, Pak Darto read it twice, folded it into a small square and slid it under the rice jar. At dinner he told his wife that the rains had come early this year, and asked for more sambal.' The text never says it directly. What does Pak Darto do with the news in the letter? Choose one word: celebrates, hides, shares.
assessment.rubric: Correct: hides: he folds the letter small, puts it under the rice jar and at dinner talks about the rain and the sambal, not the letter, so he keeps the news from his wife. 'keeps it secret' / 'keeps it to himself' = 100. 'shares' = 0 (he says nothing about it). 'celebrates' = 0 (nothing suggests good news; hiding it suggests the opposite). The idea in Indonesian ('menyembunyikannya') = 50: ask for the English word.

assessment.prompt: Read this student newspaper column (an original practice text). 'STUDENTS, REJOICE! Thanks to this year's 40% rise in fees, our university can at last afford what every student dreams of: a marble fountain at the main gate, lit in seven colours. A few ungrateful students have asked why the library now closes at 4 p.m. to save electricity. But books, as everyone knows, are on the internet, and nobody ever learnt anything by sitting somewhere quiet.' The column is ironic. Which place in the column does the writer really think needs the money? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: library: the writer mocks spending on a fountain while the library closes at 4 p.m.; 'ungrateful' and 'nobody ever learnt anything by sitting somewhere quiet' are ironic, so the real point is that the money should keep the library open. 'books' = 70 (close, but the task asks for the place). 'fountain' or 'the main gate' = 0: that is the literal reading the column mocks. 'students' or 'education' = 50 (the right direction, not the place in the text).

assessment.prompt: Read this column (an original practice text). 'OPINION · IN PRAISE OF THE JAKARTA TRAFFIC JAM. Where else could a father spend four uninterrupted hours a day with his children, all of them breathing the same rich air? Other cities waste billions on trains, which would only rob families of these precious hours together. Let us protect our jams for future generations.' Budi shares it on WhatsApp with the comment: 'At last, someone who defends traffic jams!' Budi has read the column literally. Which device has he missed? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: irony / satire: four hours in a jam, 'rich air' (= polluted air) and 'protect our jams for future generations' are absurd; the writer means the opposite and really wants trains, not jams. 'sarcasm' = 80 (close: sarcasm is a sharper, more personal irony). 'exaggeration' = 70 (a satirical technique used here, but not the whole device he missed). 'the point' or 'the joke' = 50 (the idea, without naming the device). The idea in Indonesian ('ironi', 'sindiran') = 50: ask for the English word.

assessment.prompt: Read this practice text (an original extract). 'Lebaran at my grandmother's house smelled of opor and kerosene. We slept ten to a room, a cousin's feet always in somebody's face, and woke before dawn to the sound of her broom on the yard. The house was sold years ago. I still wake early on Lebaran morning, listening for a broom.' What is the tone of the passage? Choose one: nostalgic, playful, detached, bitter.
assessment.rubric: Correct: nostalgic: warm sensory memories (the smells of opor and kerosene, the sound of the broom), a loss ('The house was sold years ago') and a longing that continues today ('I still wake early… listening for a broom'). 'wistful', 'sentimental' or 'longing' (not from the list) = 80. 'sad' = 60 (part of it, but misses the warm memory). 'playful' = 0 (one light detail about feet, but the passage is not joking). 'detached' = 0 (very personal, I and my grandmother). 'bitter' = 0 (no anger, no one is blamed).

assessment.prompt: Read this practice text (an original extract). 'The rain started at midnight. At two, water reached the door. At four, the windows. In the morning, at the evacuation centre in Bekasi, nobody spoke. Nobody needed to.' The writer builds tension and shock mainly through one feature of style. Choose one: short sentences, technical vocabulary, humorous dialogue.
assessment.rubric: Correct: short sentences: each sentence is a single quick step (midnight, two, four, the morning), like a clock ticking, and the very short last sentence ('Nobody needed to.') lands like a blow. 'repetition' = 70 (At two… At four…, nobody… Nobody: present and it helps, but it isn't one of the three choices). 'technical vocabulary' = 0 (only everyday words). 'humorous dialogue' = 0 (there is no dialogue and nothing funny).

material.title: Reading literature: narrator, character, imagery and what is implied

blocks.text:
At C1 you labelled the parts of an argument and spotted bias. Literature hides its meaning more deeply, so ask four questions.
- **Who is telling the story?** The **narrator** is the voice telling the story, and it is **not the author**. A **first-person narrator** says *I* or *we*; a **third-person narrator** says *he*, *she*, *they*. An **omniscient** (all-knowing) narrator knows every character's thoughts.
- **Can I trust the narrator?** An **unreliable narrator** tells the story in a way that we shouldn't fully believe: their words clash with their own actions or with the facts. Kazuo Ishiguro's novel *The Remains of the Day*, told by a butler who hides his own feelings from himself, is a famous example.
- **How is the character shown?** Good writers **show**, they don't **tell**: instead of *Rina was nervous*, they write what Rina does and says.
- **What is implied?** **Imagery** = words for what we see, hear, smell and touch. A **symbol** = a concrete thing that stands for an idea. Ask what a detail suggests, and **which words** show it.

id.text:
Di C1 kamu sudah menandai bagian-bagian argumen dan mengenali bias. Karya sastra menyembunyikan maknanya lebih dalam, jadi ajukan empat pertanyaan.
- **Siapa yang bercerita?** **Narator** (pencerita) adalah suara yang menceritakan kisah, dan dia **bukan pengarangnya**. **Narator orang pertama** memakai *I* atau *we* (sudut pandang aku-an); **narator orang ketiga** memakai *he*, *she*, *they* (dia-an). Narator **omniscient** (serba tahu) tahu isi pikiran semua tokoh.
- **Bisakah narator dipercaya?** **Unreliable narrator** (narator yang tidak bisa dipercaya) menceritakan kisah dengan cara yang tidak boleh kita percayai sepenuhnya: kata-katanya bertentangan dengan tindakannya sendiri atau dengan fakta. Novel Kazuo Ishiguro *The Remains of the Day*, yang diceritakan oleh seorang kepala pelayan yang menyembunyikan perasaannya bahkan dari dirinya sendiri, adalah contoh terkenal.
- **Bagaimana tokoh ditunjukkan?** Penulis yang baik **menunjukkan** (show), bukan **memberi tahu** (tell): alih-alih *Rina was nervous* (Rina gugup), mereka menulis apa yang Rina lakukan dan katakan.
- **Apa yang tersirat?** **Imagery** (citraan) = kata-kata untuk apa yang kita lihat, dengar, cium dan raba. **Simbol** = benda nyata yang mewakili sebuah gagasan. Tanyakan apa yang disiratkan sebuah detail, dan **kata mana** yang menunjukkannya.

rows.en: I was the only one in the office who stayed calm, although I may have shouted once or twice.
rows.id: Aku satu-satunya orang di kantor yang tetap tenang, walaupun mungkin aku sempat berteriak sekali atau dua kali.
rows.note: unreliable first-person narrator: the words clash with the actions

id.note: narator orang pertama yang tidak bisa dipercaya: kata-katanya bertentangan dengan tindakannya

rows.note: telling: the writer simply names the feeling

id.note: memberi tahu (telling): penulis langsung menyebut perasaannya

rows.en: Rina read the first line of her speech for the fifth time and checked again that her phone was on silent.
rows.id: Rina membaca baris pertama pidatonya untuk kelima kalinya dan memeriksa lagi bahwa HP-nya dalam mode senyap.
rows.note: showing: her actions tell us she is nervous

id.note: menunjukkan (showing): tindakannya memberi tahu kita bahwa dia gugup

rows.en: 'Congratulations,' said her brother, and went back to his phone.
rows.id: 'Selamat,' kata kakaknya, lalu kembali ke HP-nya.
rows.note: dialogue + action: the word is kind, the action is cold

id.note: dialog + tindakan: katanya ramah, tindakannya dingin

rows.en: The banyan tree in the square had stood there longer than the town itself.
rows.id: Pohon beringin di alun-alun itu sudah berdiri di sana lebih lama daripada kota itu sendiri.
rows.note: a possible symbol: something old and lasting, if the story returns to it

id.note: kemungkinan simbol: sesuatu yang tua dan bertahan, kalau cerita kembali kepadanya

blocks.text:
**You already know the tools from Bahasa Indonesia class**: *sudut pandang orang pertama / ketiga*, *majas* (metafora, perumpamaan, personifikasi, hiperbola, ironi) and *makna tersirat*. Pramoedya's *Bumi Manusia*, for example, is told in the first person by Minke.
**Two traps.** (1) Treating the narrator as the author, or the narrator's opinion as the truth: an *I* in a novel is a character. (2) Turning every object into a symbol. A detail is probably a symbol only if the story **repeats** it, places it at a **key moment** or links it to the **theme**. Otherwise, a chair is just a chair.

id.text:
**Kamu sudah kenal alatnya dari pelajaran Bahasa Indonesia**: *sudut pandang orang pertama / ketiga*, *majas* (metafora, perumpamaan, personifikasi, hiperbola, ironi) dan *makna tersirat*. *Bumi Manusia* karya Pramoedya, misalnya, diceritakan oleh Minke dengan sudut pandang orang pertama.
**Dua jebakan.** (1) Menganggap narator sebagai pengarang, atau pendapat narator sebagai kebenaran: *I* dalam novel adalah seorang tokoh. (2) Menjadikan setiap benda sebagai simbol. Sebuah detail kemungkinan besar simbol hanya kalau cerita **mengulanginya**, menaruhnya di **momen penting** atau mengaitkannya dengan **tema**. Kalau tidak, kursi ya hanya kursi.

blocks.prompt: A practice text: 'Dimas said he was happy for his friend, and kept stirring a coffee he had already finished.' What does the action suggest?
options: Dimas is not really happy for his friend.
Dimas is too busy to talk.
blocks.explain: This is **showing**: he *says* he's happy, but stirring an empty cup is a nervous, distracted action, so his feelings don't match his words. Nothing suggests he wants more coffee or is busy.

id.prompt: Sebuah teks latihan: 'Dimas said he was happy for his friend, and kept stirring a coffee he had already finished.' Apa yang disiratkan oleh tindakannya?
id.explain: Ini **showing** (menunjukkan): dia *bilang* dia ikut senang, tetapi mengaduk cangkir yang sudah kosong adalah tindakan gelisah dan tidak fokus, jadi perasaannya tidak sesuai dengan kata-katanya. Tidak ada yang menyiratkan dia mau kopi lagi atau sedang sibuk.

id.title: Membaca karya sastra: narator, tokoh, citraan dan yang tersirat

material.title: Philosophical essays: following an abstract argument

blocks.text:
A **philosophical essay** argues about an abstract question (What is a promise? Are we responsible for luck? Is it ever right to lie?). It is built from a few **moves**, and each move has its **signposts** (phrases that tell you what the sentence is doing):
- **Definition**: the writer fixes the meaning of a key word. *By X I mean…*, *Let us call this…*
- **Thought experiment**: an invented case to test our intuitions. *Imagine…*, *Suppose…*, *Consider a case in which…* (the famous *trolley problem* is one).
- **Objection**: a view against the writer's. *It might be objected that…*, *Some will say…*, *A critic may reply that…*
- **Reply**: the writer's answer. *I grant that…, but…*, *This objection fails because…*, *But this assumes…*
- **Conclusion**: *It follows that…*, *If this is right, then…*
**How to read it:** slowly. After each paragraph, stop and paraphrase it in one plain sentence (*So he's saying that…*). Ask what each sentence **does** in the argument, not just what it says.

id.text:
**Esai filosofis** berargumen tentang pertanyaan abstrak (Apa itu janji? Apakah kita bertanggung jawab atas nasib baik atau buruk? Apakah berbohong pernah dibenarkan?). Esai ini dibangun dari beberapa **langkah** (moves), dan setiap langkah punya **penanda** (frasa yang memberi tahu apa yang sedang dilakukan kalimat itu):
- **Definition** (definisi): penulis menetapkan arti kata kunci. *By X I mean…* (yang saya maksud dengan X adalah…), *Let us call this…* (sebut saja ini…)
- **Thought experiment** (eksperimen pikiran): kasus rekaan untuk menguji intuisi kita. *Imagine…*, *Suppose…* (misalkan…), *Consider a case in which…* (*trolley problem* yang terkenal adalah salah satunya).
- **Objection** (sanggahan): pandangan yang menentang penulis. *It might be objected that…* (mungkin ada yang menyanggah bahwa…), *Some will say…*, *A critic may reply that…*
- **Reply** (jawaban): jawaban penulis. *I grant that…, but…* (saya akui bahwa…, tetapi…), *This objection fails because…*, *But this assumes…* (tetapi ini mengandaikan…)
- **Conclusion** (kesimpulan): *It follows that…* (maka…), *If this is right, then…*
**Cara membacanya:** pelan-pelan. Setelah setiap paragraf, berhenti dan parafrasekan dalam satu kalimat sederhana (*Jadi dia bilang bahwa…*). Tanyakan apa yang **dilakukan** setiap kalimat dalam argumen, bukan hanya apa yang dikatakannya.

blocks.text:
**The C1 trap, again.** *It might be objected that…* and *Some will say…* introduce the **other side**, not the writer's view. Expect a reply soon after.
**'I grant that' is not surrender.** The writer agrees with a small point to make the reply stronger: *I grant that…, but…* = *Memang…, tetapi…*.
**Abstract nouns pile up** (*the moral significance of the consequences of an action*). Unpack them into a simple sentence: *whether what happens after we act changes how good or bad the act was*.
**the former / the latter** = the first / the second of two things just mentioned (*yang pertama / yang terakhir*).

id.text:
**Jebakan C1, lagi.** *It might be objected that…* dan *Some will say…* memperkenalkan **pihak lain**, bukan pandangan penulis. Tunggu jawabannya tidak lama kemudian.
**'I grant that' bukan menyerah.** Penulis setuju dengan satu poin kecil supaya jawabannya lebih kuat: *I grant that…, but…* = *Memang…, tetapi…*.
**Kata benda abstrak menumpuk** (*the moral significance of the consequences of an action*). Uraikan menjadi kalimat sederhana: *apakah apa yang terjadi setelah kita bertindak mengubah seberapa baik atau buruk tindakan itu*.
**the former / the latter** = yang pertama / yang terakhir dari dua hal yang baru disebut.

id.title: Esai filosofis: mengikuti argumen yang abstrak

blocks.text:
**Satire** mocks a real problem to make a serious point. Three techniques:
- **Saying the opposite** of what you mean (**irony**): *Congratulations to the council on another year without a single new pavement.*
- **Exaggeration to absurdity**: the writer pushes an idea until it becomes ridiculous.
- **A mock-serious (deadpan) tone**: a crazy proposal in calm, official language, with numbers, permits and procedures.
**Clues that a column is ironic:** an absurd **headline**; proposals that nobody could mean; **contradictions**; absurd logic; a real problem described as a good thing; and the column's name (some newspapers have a regular humour column).
The classic example is Jonathan Swift's *A Modest Proposal* (1729), which calmly suggested that poor Irish families sell their babies as food for the rich. Swift didn't want anyone eaten: he was attacking how the powerful treated the Irish poor. Writers still use the phrase **a modest proposal** as a wink that satire is coming. George Orwell's *Animal Farm* is satire as a story.

id.text:
**Satire** mengejek masalah nyata untuk menyampaikan maksud yang serius. Tiga tekniknya:
- **Mengatakan kebalikan** dari maksudnya (**ironi**): *Congratulations to the council on another year without a single new pavement* (selamat untuk dewan kota atas satu tahun lagi tanpa satu pun trotoar baru).
- **Melebih-lebihkan sampai absurd**: penulis mendorong sebuah ide sampai jadi konyol.
- **Nada pura-pura serius (deadpan)**: usul yang gila dengan bahasa yang tenang dan resmi, lengkap dengan angka, izin dan prosedur.
**Petunjuk bahwa sebuah kolom ironis:** **judul** yang absurd; usul yang tidak mungkin dimaksudkan sungguh-sungguh; **kontradiksi**; logika yang absurd; masalah nyata yang digambarkan sebagai hal baik; dan nama kolomnya (beberapa koran punya kolom humor tetap).
Contoh klasiknya adalah *A Modest Proposal* (1729) karya Jonathan Swift, yang dengan tenang mengusulkan agar keluarga miskin Irlandia menjual bayi mereka sebagai makanan bagi orang kaya. Swift tentu tidak ingin ada yang dimakan: dia menyerang cara orang-orang berkuasa memperlakukan rakyat miskin Irlandia. Penulis masih memakai frasa **a modest proposal** (usul sederhana) sebagai kedipan mata bahwa satire akan datang. *Animal Farm* karya George Orwell adalah satire dalam bentuk cerita.

blocks.text:
**The danger: reading satire literally.** Satirical articles are often shared as if they were real news, and readers get angry at writers who in fact agree with them. Before you react, ask: *Could anyone really mean this? What is the real problem behind it?* The real point is usually the **opposite** of the literal proposal.
**Indonesian link:** you know *sindiran* and the *majas ironi, sinisme, sarkasme*. English satire is often **drier**: no emoji, no *wkwk*, no wink, just a straight face. The calmer the language, the louder the joke.
**Don't decide from one word.** One *great* or *wonderful* isn't enough: check the whole text against the facts.
**British vs American:** *pavement* (UK) = *sidewalk* (US).

id.text:
**Bahayanya: membaca satire secara harfiah.** Artikel satire sering dibagikan seolah-olah berita sungguhan, dan pembaca marah kepada penulis yang sebenarnya sependapat dengan mereka. Sebelum bereaksi, tanyakan: *Mungkinkah ada orang yang sungguh-sungguh bermaksud begini? Apa masalah nyata di baliknya?* Maksud sebenarnya biasanya **kebalikan** dari usul harfiahnya.
**Hubungannya dengan bahasa Indonesia:** kamu kenal *sindiran* dan *majas ironi, sinisme, sarkasme*. Satire bahasa Inggris sering lebih **kering**: tanpa emoji, tanpa *wkwk*, tanpa kedipan mata, hanya wajah datar. Makin tenang bahasanya, makin keras leluconnya.
**Jangan memutuskan dari satu kata.** Satu kata *great* atau *wonderful* belum cukup: cek seluruh teks terhadap faktanya.
**Inggris vs Amerika:** *pavement* (Inggris) = *sidewalk* (Amerika) = trotoar.

blocks.prompt: A headline: 'Ministry to fix potholes by officially renaming them speed features.' What is this?
options: A real report about a new road policy
Satire about fixing words instead of fixing roads

blocks.explain: Renaming a hole doesn't fix it: the idea is absurd, but it is said in official language (*officially renaming*). That's satire. The real point: the authorities change the words instead of solving the problem.

material.title: Author's style: how it creates tone

blocks.text:
**Style** = how a writer writes. Five features to look at:
- **Sentence length and rhythm**: short sentences create tension, shock or finality; long, flowing sentences suit memory, calm or a flood of feeling.
- **Word choice and register**: warm everyday words, cold technical words, official language, slang.
- **Figurative language**: *simile* (like / as: *quiet as a closed shop*), *metaphor* (*the city is a pressure cooker*), *personification* (things acting like people: *the shutter refused to close*).
- **Repetition**: a word or pattern that comes back builds rhythm and emphasis.
- **Point of view**: *I* feels close and personal; a distant third person can feel cool.
These create the **tone**: the writer's **attitude**. Useful tone words: **nostalgic** (warm and longing for the past), **bitter** (angry and hurt, blaming someone), **playful** (light, joking), **detached** (cool, distant, only facts), **critical** (showing disapproval).
**Mood** is different: it is how the **reader** feels (tense, peaceful, uneasy).

id.text:
**Gaya** = cara penulis menulis. Lima ciri yang perlu diperhatikan:
- **Panjang dan irama kalimat**: kalimat pendek membangun ketegangan, kejutan atau kesan final; kalimat panjang yang mengalir cocok untuk kenangan, ketenangan atau perasaan yang meluap.
- **Pilihan kata dan ragam bahasa (register)**: kata sehari-hari yang hangat, kata teknis yang dingin, bahasa resmi, bahasa gaul.
- **Bahasa kiasan (majas)**: *simile* (perumpamaan, pakai like / as: *quiet as a closed shop*), *metafora* (*the city is a pressure cooker*), *personifikasi* (benda bertindak seperti manusia: *the shutter refused to close*).
- **Pengulangan (repetisi)**: kata atau pola yang muncul lagi membangun irama dan penekanan.
- **Sudut pandang**: *I* terasa dekat dan pribadi; orang ketiga yang berjarak bisa terasa dingin.
Semua ini membangun **nada (tone)**: **sikap** penulis. Kata nada yang berguna: **nostalgic** (hangat dan merindukan masa lalu), **bitter** (getir: marah dan sakit hati, menyalahkan seseorang), **playful** (jenaka, ringan, bercanda), **detached** (dingin, berjarak, hanya fakta), **critical** (menunjukkan ketidaksetujuan).
**Mood (suasana)** berbeda: itu yang dirasakan **pembaca** (tegang, damai, gelisah).

id.note: detached (berjarak): hanya fakta, tidak ada perasaan yang disebut

blocks.text:
**Name the feature, the effect and the words.** Not *The tone is sad*, but *The short sentences and the repeated 'then' create a tense tone*.
**Don't mix up tone words.** A sad text isn't automatically **bitter**: bitter needs anger and someone to blame. A calm text isn't automatically **detached**: detached means the writer keeps their feelings out of it.
**Detached can still say a lot.** *Two hundred workers were informed by email* names no feelings, but putting that fact last invites the reader to judge.
**Indonesian habit:** formal Indonesian writing often joins ideas in long sentences. In English, a sudden short sentence is a deliberate choice: notice it.

id.text:
**Sebutkan cirinya, efeknya dan kata-katanya.** Bukan *Nadanya sedih*, tetapi *Kalimat-kalimat pendek dan pengulangan 'then' menciptakan nada yang tegang*.
**Jangan tertukar kata nada.** Teks yang sedih belum tentu **bitter**: bitter perlu kemarahan dan seseorang yang disalahkan. Teks yang tenang belum tentu **detached**: detached berarti penulis menjauhkan perasaannya dari tulisan.
**Yang berjarak pun bisa banyak berbicara.** *Two hundred workers were informed by email* tidak menyebut perasaan, tetapi menaruh fakta itu di akhir mengajak pembaca menilai.
**Kebiasaan bahasa Indonesia:** tulisan resmi bahasa Indonesia sering menggabungkan ide dalam kalimat panjang. Dalam bahasa Inggris, kalimat pendek yang tiba-tiba adalah pilihan yang disengaja: perhatikan itu.

blocks.prompt: A practice text: 'The village was flooded on Tuesday. Forty houses were damaged. The relief truck arrived on Friday.' Which tone word fits best?
blocks.explain: Short factual sentences, no *I*, no feelings named: the writer keeps their distance, so the tone is **detached**. There are no memories (nostalgic) and no jokes (playful). The fact placed last (*Friday*, three days later) may still make the reader judge.

id.prompt: Sebuah teks latihan: 'The village was flooded on Tuesday. Forty houses were damaged. The relief truck arrived on Friday.' Kata nada mana yang paling cocok?
id.explain: Kalimat faktual yang pendek, tanpa *I*, tanpa perasaan yang disebut: penulis menjaga jarak, jadi nadanya **detached**. Tidak ada kenangan (nostalgic) dan tidak ada lelucon (playful). Fakta yang ditaruh terakhir (*Friday*, tiga hari kemudian) tetap bisa membuat pembaca menilai.

assessment.rl-1: Baca teks latihan ini (kutipan orisinal yang ditulis untuk pelajaran ini). 'Nobody could call me careless with money. This year I bought only three phones, each of them a bargain, and I cancelled my gym membership the moment I noticed I had not been for eleven months. My sister keeps telling me to make a budget. I don't need one: I remember everything I spend, roughly.' Narator jenis apa ini? Pilih satu, dalam bahasa Inggris: omniscient narrator, reliable narrator, unreliable narrator.
assessment.rl-2: Baca kutipan dari sebuah esai filosofis ini (teks latihan orisinal). '(A) By a promise I mean words that give another person the right to expect something from us. (B) Suppose you promise a dying friend that you will scatter his ashes at sea, and afterwards you simply keep them on a shelf. (C) Some will say that nothing wrong has happened, since your friend can no longer be disappointed. (D) But this assumes that promises matter only because of how people feel; if that were true, a secret betrayal would be no betrayal at all.' Kalimat (C) adalah langkah apa dalam argumen ini? Pilih satu, dalam bahasa Inggris: definition, thought experiment, objection, reply.
assessment.rl-3: Baca teks latihan ini (kutipan pendek orisinal). 'When the letter from the hospital came, Pak Darto read it twice, folded it into a small square and slid it under the rice jar. At dinner he told his wife that the rains had come early this year, and asked for more sambal.' Teks ini tidak mengatakannya secara langsung. Apa yang dilakukan Pak Darto dengan kabar di surat itu? Pilih satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris: celebrates, hides, shares.
assessment.rl-4: Baca kolom koran mahasiswa ini (teks latihan orisinal). 'STUDENTS, REJOICE! Thanks to this year's 40% rise in fees, our university can at last afford what every student dreams of: a marble fountain at the main gate, lit in seven colours. A few ungrateful students have asked why the library now closes at 4 p.m. to save electricity. But books, as everyone knows, are on the internet, and nobody ever learnt anything by sitting somewhere quiet.' Kolom ini ironis. Tempat mana di kolom ini yang menurut penulis sebenarnya membutuhkan uang itu? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.rl-5: Baca kolom ini (teks latihan orisinal). 'OPINION · IN PRAISE OF THE JAKARTA TRAFFIC JAM. Where else could a father spend four uninterrupted hours a day with his children, all of them breathing the same rich air? Other cities waste billions on trains, which would only rob families of these precious hours together. Let us protect our jams for future generations.' Budi membagikannya di WhatsApp dengan komentar: 'At last, someone who defends traffic jams!' Budi membaca kolom ini secara harfiah. Gaya bahasa (device) apa yang dia lewatkan? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.rl-6: Baca teks latihan ini (kutipan orisinal). 'Lebaran at my grandmother's house smelled of opor and kerosene. We slept ten to a room, a cousin's feet always in somebody's face, and woke before dawn to the sound of her broom on the yard. The house was sold years ago. I still wake early on Lebaran morning, listening for a broom.' Apa nada (tone) teks ini? Pilih satu, dalam bahasa Inggris: nostalgic, playful, detached, bitter.
assessment.rl-7: Baca teks latihan ini (kutipan orisinal). 'The rain started at midnight. At two, water reached the door. At four, the windows. In the morning, at the evacuation centre in Bekasi, nobody spoke. Nobody needed to.' Penulis membangun ketegangan dan rasa terkejut terutama lewat satu ciri gaya. Pilih satu, dalam bahasa Inggris: short sentences, technical vocabulary, humorous dialogue.
